Further along the same rim, two slender adults — one in quilted ember-orange, one in indigo — share a single acorn cup of something steaming, neither looking at the sky, their leaf-veined wings folded tight, both entirely unashamed.

Back at the rim, a long-limbed man in a plum hooded cape lies flat on the moss with one arm over his face, plainly having given up, a grass cord still knotted round three fingers, his amber wings crooked upward.

Out on the branch behind, a real moth — wings open, motionless, enormous against their scale — has settled squarely across the moss pad, and three adults in teal and moss-green stand with arms folded at a respectful distance, waiting it out.

Further along the surface, a narrow-shouldered woman in a lichen cape is halfway up a stem with a brass-headed pin held between her teeth, her long copper hair loose, her dragonfly-clear wings angled out for balance, both hands gripping bark.

Down the slope, a long-legged man wrapped in a blanket of woven milkweed floss with only a sharp jaw and a pointed ear showing is still pushing pins into a moss pad, his moth-furred violet wings tenting the blanket from behind.

Back at the rim, two adults hold a third woman by both ankles while she leans past the edge with both arms completely free and all three of them shout different things, the middle one holding on with exactly one finger, wings splayed.

Further back on the branch, one tall man has climbed higher than anyone needed to and stands on the very topmost twig with his hands on his hips, his teal jerkin bright, his leaf-veined wings spread, deeply pleased with the altitude.

Out behind, a real hedgehog is asleep against the side of the moss pad being used as a windbreak, and one slender woman in rose-red bark-cloth crouches beside it deciding with great seriousness whether to move it or simply work around it.

Further along the same surface, one long-limbed woman in an indigo quilted coat is counting on her long fingers, loses count, closes her fist, starts again, her sea-glass wings trembling with each small frustrated exhale, a bead on a grass cord waiting in her other hand.

Back at the rim, a real owl sits on the branch above and watches them all with its eyes half-closed and its whole bearing one long slow judgment, a single amber-winged adult beneath it studiously admiring the sky instead.

Down the slope a little, a slender woman in a moss-green cape is running back with a fresh dewdrop cupped in both hands, going with extraordinary care, her long dark braid flying sideways, her moth-furred wings working hard to slow her down.

Further along the branch, two long-legged adults in overlapping lichen hoods bend over the same moss pad and point at two completely different places in the sky with whole outstretched arms, a third between them resting her chin in her hands and waiting.

Back at the rim, a slender man in a plum and ember-orange quilted jerkin is trying to persuade a real beetle to stand still on a thread crossing his moss pad, the beetle uninterested, his dragonfly-clear wings fanned out in exasperation.

Further along the same surface, the whole line of them has put every scrap of work down and turned the wrong way entirely, all staring at something behind them, a single half-pushed pin standing in the moss, nobody minding it.

Out on the branch behind, a long-limbed man in a teal bark-cloth coat has one foot on a seed cap and is mid-slip, arms wide, a coloured cord unwinding from his wrist in a long spiral, his leaf-veined wings snapping open too late.

Further back, a real dormouse is curled inside an upturned acorn cap directly beside the moss work, asleep, and one narrow-shouldered woman in apricot down-cloth leans over it with a hand pressed to her mouth, delighted, her pointed ears angled forward.

Down the slope, two adults in indigo and rose share the work of holding a grass cord taut between them, both leaning back hard against the tension, their wings wide for counterweight, both grinning at the precise angle they have made.

Further along the rim, one slender woman in a cream and violet layered cape has wrapped herself in an extra scarf of milkweed floss until only her long nose and pointed ears are visible, but her moth-furred wings are still spread and working.

Back at the rim, a tall man in ember-orange has climbed a stem purely to be higher than the woman beside him and is already discovering the advantage is smaller than he imagined, his bark boots losing grip, his teal wings flaring.

Further out on the branch, one long-legged woman in quilted moss-green sits with her back to all the work, arms crossed, chin lifted, magnificently done with the whole project, a snail crossing the toe of her shaped-bark boot entirely beneath her attention.

Down the slope, a slender man in an indigo jerkin and high bark boots is wound so tightly in his own grass cord that both arms are pinned to his sides, and a second adult in plum cloth stands over him offering commentary instead of help, arms folded.

Further along the surface, three adults in teal, rose and amber have all turned at once to look at the same bead rolling away across the bark and nobody has caught it yet, all three reaching in slightly different directions.

Out on the branch behind, a real glow-worm has settled on the rim of the moss pad and the two adults working nearest it have quietly repositioned their whole arrangement to use its light, neither acknowledging to the other what they have done.

Further back, a narrow-shouldered woman in an overlapping lichen cape sits with a pad of moss across her knees and every pin in it has fallen sideways in the same direction, a small disaster she is staring at with both hands raised.

Back at the rim, a long-limbed man in quilted violet with owl-down collar and cuffs is fast asleep sitting up, a coloured thread still wound round one raised finger, and a second adult crouches in front of him deciding with professional interest whether he knew anything useful anyway.
